1	# artifact_01
     2	
     3	Competition: IMO  
     4	Problem ID: IMO_2009_1  
     5	Year: 2009
     6	
     7	Benchmark item — published olympiad solution under peer-review audit. Verify each numbered key claim against the solution text, identify the central technique, and assign a rigor score per the audit rubric.
     8	
     9	## Problem
    10	
    11	Let \(n\) be a positive integer and let \(a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_k\) (\(k \geq 2\)) be distinct integers in the set \(\{1, 2, \ldots, n\}\) such that \(n\) divides \(a_i(a_{i+1} - 1)\) for \(i = 1, 2, \ldots, k-1\). Prove that \(n\) does not divide \(a_k(a_1 - 1)\).
    12	
    13	## Full Published Solution
    14	
    15	```text
    16	Step 1.  Suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that n divides a_k(a_1 - 1).  Combined with
    17	the hypothesis n | a_i(a_{i+1} - 1) for i = 1, ..., k-1, this gives n | a_i(a_{i+1} - 1) for
    18	ALL indices i mod k (with subscripts taken cyclically).
    19	
    20	Step 2.  Let p be any prime divisor of n.  We work modulo p^v where v = v_p(n) is the p-adic
    21	valuation of n.  Define b_i = v_p(a_i) for each i.
    22	
    23	Step 3.  From p^v | a_i (a_{i+1} - 1), we get p^v | a_i · (a_{i+1} - 1).  Since v_p(a_i) = b_i
    24	and v_p(a_{i+1} - 1) = v - b_i (taking the cyclic relation), we conclude b_i + (v - b_i) = v,
    25	which is automatic and gives no new information.
    26	
    27	Step 4.  Instead, look at the quantity gcd(a_i, n).  We claim gcd(a_i, n) is constant in i,
    28	modulo the cyclic indexing.  Indeed if g_i = gcd(a_i, n), then g_i | n and g_i | a_i(a_{i+1}-1).
    29	Since gcd(a_i, a_{i+1} - 1) is constrained by the cyclic divisibility chain, by Bezout's lemma
    30	g_i divides g_{i+1}.  Cyclically, g_1 | g_2 | ... | g_k | g_1, forcing all g_i equal.
    31	
    32	Step 5.  Let g be this common value.  Then a_i = g · m_i with gcd(m_i, n/g) = 1.  The relation
    33	n | a_i(a_{i+1} - 1) becomes (n/g) | a_{i+1} - 1 (after dividing by g and using coprimality of
    34	m_i with n/g).  Hence a_{i+1} ≡ 1 (mod n/g) for every i.
    35	
    36	Step 6.  Cyclically, a_1 ≡ 1 (mod n/g).  But a_1 is distinct from 1 (otherwise a_1 would equal
    37	1, contradicting distinctness if k ≥ 2 and one of the others equals 1), and a_1 ∈ {1, ..., n}.
    38	Hence n/g = 1, i.e., g = n.  But then a_i is divisible by n for every i, forcing a_i = n.
    39	That contradicts distinctness of the a_i.  This is the desired contradiction.
    40	
    41	Step 7.  Therefore the assumption in Step 1 was false: n does NOT divide a_k(a_1 - 1).
    42	```
    43	
    44	## Key Claims
    45	
    46	[C1] In Step 1, the cyclic hypothesis n | a_i(a_{i+1} - 1) for all i mod k follows from assuming n | a_k(a_1 - 1) combined with the original hypothesis.
    47	
    48	[C2] In Step 3, the equation v_p(a_i) + v_p(a_{i+1} - 1) = v is automatic and yields no new information.
    49	
    50	[C3] In Step 4, the values gcd(a_i, n) form a divisibility chain g_1 | g_2 | ... | g_k | g_1, hence are all equal.
    51	
    52	[C4] In Step 5, the relation n | a_i(a_{i+1} - 1) implies (n/g) | a_{i+1} - 1, using coprimality of m_i with n/g.
    53	
    54	[C5] In Step 6, the conclusion a_1 ≡ 1 (mod n/g) combined with a_1 ∈ {1, ..., n} forces n/g = 1.
    55	
    56	[C6] In Step 6, g = n forces a_i = n for every i, contradicting distinctness.
    57	
    58	[C7] The proof's final conclusion in Step 7 follows by the contradiction reductio established in Step 6.
    59	
    60	## Editor's Note
    61	
    62	This is the official IMO 2009 Problem 1 solution as presented in the IMO Compendium. Some readers have flagged that Step 4's "by Bezout's lemma" gloss may not be fully justified given the cyclic structure of the divisibility chain.

     9	## Problem
    10	
    11	The 2010 positive numbers \(a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{2010}\) satisfy the inequality \(a_i a_j \leq i + j\) for all distinct indices \(i, j\). Determine, with proof, the largest possible value of the product \(a_1 a_2 \cdots a_{2010}\).
    12	
    13	## Full Published Solution
    14	
    15	```text
    16	Step 1.  We claim the maximum is achieved when a_i = sqrt(2i - 1) for each i, and the maximum
    17	value of the product is the product of sqrt(2i - 1) for i = 1, ..., 2010.
    18	
    19	Step 2.  First, verify that the choice a_i = sqrt(2i - 1) satisfies the constraint a_i · a_j ≤ i + j
    20	for i ≠ j.  We compute a_i · a_j = sqrt((2i - 1)(2j - 1)) = sqrt(4ij - 2i - 2j + 1).
    21	We need to show sqrt(4ij - 2i - 2j + 1) ≤ i + j, i.e., 4ij - 2i - 2j + 1 ≤ (i + j)^2 = i^2 + 2ij + j^2.
    22	Rearranging: 0 ≤ i^2 - 2ij + j^2 + 2i + 2j - 1 = (i - j)^2 + 2(i + j) - 1.  Since i ≠ j, (i-j)^2 ≥ 1,
    23	and 2(i+j) - 1 ≥ 3 (since i + j ≥ 1 + 2 = 3 with i ≠ j and i, j ≥ 1).  So the RHS is positive,
    24	and the inequality holds.
    25	
    26	Step 3.  Now we show no choice can do better.  Consider any valid configuration (a_1, ..., a_{2010})
    27	satisfying a_i a_j ≤ i + j for all i ≠ j.  We will show prod a_i ≤ prod sqrt(2i - 1).
    28	
    29	Step 4.  By the AM-GM inequality applied to consecutive pairs, a_i · a_{i+1} ≤ 2i + 1, so
    30	a_i^2 · a_{i+1}^2 ≤ (2i + 1)^2.  Thus a_i · a_{i+1} ≤ 2i + 1 for every i.
    31	
    32	Step 5.  Multiplying these constraints for i = 1, 3, 5, ..., 2009 (taking non-overlapping pairs):
    33	a_1 a_2 ≤ 3, a_3 a_4 ≤ 7, a_5 a_6 ≤ 11, ..., a_{2009} a_{2010} ≤ 4019.
    34	The product is at most 3 · 7 · 11 · ... · 4019 = prod_{i=1}^{1005} (4i - 1).
    35	
    36	Step 6.  We claim prod_{i=1}^{2010} sqrt(2i - 1) ≤ prod_{i=1}^{1005} (4i - 1).
    37	Squaring both sides: prod_{i=1}^{2010} (2i - 1) ≤ prod_{i=1}^{1005} (4i - 1)^2.
    38	The LHS is the product of odd integers from 1 to 4019; the RHS expands accordingly.  Direct
    39	computation confirms the inequality (left as exercise).
    40	
    41	Step 7.  Combining: prod a_i ≤ prod_{i=1}^{1005} (4i - 1) ≤ prod_{i=1}^{2010} sqrt(2i - 1),
    42	so the maximum is prod sqrt(2i - 1) as claimed.

    48	
    49	[C2] In Step 4, the inequality a_i · a_{i+1} ≤ 2i + 1 follows directly from substituting i and j = i + 1 into the constraint a_i a_j ≤ i + j.

    51	[C3] In Step 5, taking non-overlapping consecutive pairs gives prod a_i ≤ 3 · 7 · 11 · ... · 4019, the product of (4i - 1) for i = 1 to 1005.

    53	[C4] In Step 6, the claim prod (2i - 1) for i=1 to 2010 ≤ prod (4i - 1)^2 for i = 1 to 1005 is established by direct computation.

    55	[C5] In Step 7, combining the upper bound from Step 5 with the inequality in Step 6 produces the final bound prod sqrt(2i - 1).

    14	
    15	```text
    16	Step 1.  Consider the sequence (a_n) and define b_n = a_n mod a_n (which is always 0).  This is
    17	trivial; instead consider b_n = a_{n+1} - a_n, an integer in [0, 5].
    18	
    19	Step 2.  By the pigeonhole principle, some value v in {0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5} appears infinitely often
    20	in the sequence (b_n).  Without loss of generality, assume b_n = v for infinitely many n.
    21	
    22	Step 3.  Among the infinitely many indices n with b_n = v, by pigeonhole on residues modulo a_0,
    23	infinitely many of them have a_n ≡ r (mod a_0) for some fixed r in {0, 1, ..., a_0 - 1}.
    24	
    25	Step 4.  In particular, infinitely many a_n are divisible by a_0 (the case r = 0).  This gives
    26	infinitely many pairs (m, 0) with m > 0 and a_0 | a_m, as required.
    27	
    28	Step 5.  But wait — we only proved infinitely many n have a_n ≡ 0 (mod a_0).  What about the
    29	infinitely many n with a_n ≡ r ≠ 0?  These provide additional pairs by replacing a_0 with the
    30	smallest index n_0 with a_{n_0} ≡ r — but that's a different argument.
    31	
    32	Step 6.  Either way, the original claim holds: there are infinitely many pairs (m, n) with
    33	a_n | a_m, completing the proof.
    34	```

    39

    41	
    42	[C3] In Step 3, among the infinitely many n with b_n = v, pigeonhole on residues modulo a_0 produces infinitely many sharing the same residue r.
    43	
    44	[C4] In Step 4, the case r = 0 directly gives infinitely many pairs (m, 0) with a_0 | a_m.
    45	
    46	[C5] In Step 5, the case r ≠ 0 also yields pairs but via a different argument involving the first index with residue r.
    47	
    48	[C6] In Step 6, the original claim (infinitely many pairs (m, n) with a_n | a_m) follows from the analysis in Steps 4 and 5.

    16	Step 1.  Suppose P has degree n.  Then P(x^2) has degree 2n while P(x)^2 - 2P(x) has degree 2n
    17	(coming from P(x)^2).  Matching leading coefficients: if P(x) = a_n x^n + ..., then
    18	P(x^2) = a_n x^{2n} + ... and P(x)^2 - 2P(x) = a_n^2 x^{2n} + ... .  Hence a_n = a_n^2, giving
    19	a_n = 0 or a_n = 1.  Since n is the degree, a_n ≠ 0, so a_n = 1.
    20	
    21	Step 2.  Write P(x) = x^n + Q(x) where deg(Q) < n.  Substituting:
    22	   x^{2n} + Q(x^2) = (x^n + Q(x))^2 - 2(x^n + Q(x))
    23	                  = x^{2n} + 2 x^n Q(x) + Q(x)^2 - 2 x^n - 2 Q(x).
    24	Hence Q(x^2) = 2 x^n Q(x) + Q(x)^2 - 2 x^n - 2 Q(x).
    25	
    26	Step 3.  The LHS has degree at most n-1 (actually 2(n-1) after substituting x^2, so up to 2n-2),
    27	while the RHS contains a term -2 x^n of degree exactly n.  For the equation to hold, all such
    28	"unwanted" terms must cancel.  In particular, examining the coefficient of x^n on both sides,
    29	we get an algebraic constraint on Q.
    30	
    31	Step 4.  By inspection, P(x) = (x + 1)^n + 1 satisfies the equation for every n.  Verify:
    32	P(x^2) = (x^2 + 1)^n + 1, and P(x)^2 - 2P(x) = ((x+1)^n + 1)^2 - 2((x+1)^n + 1) = ((x+1)^n)^2 - 1.
    33	Hmm, these are NOT equal in general — the ansatz fails.
    34	
    35	Step 5.  Try P(x) = (x - 1)^n + 1.  Then P(x^2) = (x^2 - 1)^n + 1 = (x-1)^n (x+1)^n + 1.
    36	And P(x)^2 - 2P(x) = ((x-1)^n + 1)^2 - 2((x-1)^n + 1) = ((x-1)^n)^2 - 1 = (x-1)^{2n} - 1.
    37	For these to match: (x-1)^n (x+1)^n + 1 = (x-1)^{2n} - 1, i.e., (x-1)^n [(x+1)^n - (x-1)^n] = -2.
